1.title: Know what a portfolio is and what the words mean
1.intro: This course is about how portfolio management work is done. It is education, not personal advice. Consult a licensed professional for your own money.
pts: Explain that a portfolio is a set of investments held together for a goal.
Name the main asset types: cash, bonds, shares and funds.
Explain risk as the chance that results differ from what you hoped.
Explain return, fees and time frame in plain words.
Say clearly that managing money for others is a regulated activity.
1.ex: A portfolio holds cash for next year's needs, bonds for steadier income and shares for long-term growth. Each part has a different job.
1.act: Write a one-page glossary of ten terms and explain it aloud to a friend.
1.std: Task: define ten portfolio terms. Condition: own words, one page. Standard: each term is correct and a friend can repeat it back.

2.title: Know the rules and who may do this work
2.intro: Managing money for other people is regulated in Canada. Know the line before you cross it.
pts: Explain that advising on or managing investments for others usually requires registration with the provincial securities regulator.
Check the current rule with your provincial regulator before you offer any service.
Explain that a firm must know its client and check that each investment suits the client.
Explain the duty to put the client's interest first and to tell about conflicts.
Explain anti-money-laundering rules: know your client, keep records, report suspicious activity.
2.ex: A person wants to start 'managing friends' money' for a fee. The right step is to ask the regulator what registration is needed first, not to begin.
2.act: Make a rules table with rule, who enforces it, what it requires and the source with date.
2.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: official regulator pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a dated source; no rule is guessed.

3.title: Know the client: goals, time frame and comfort with risk
3.intro: A portfolio starts with the person, not the product. This is how professionals gather facts.
pts: Ask about goals, time frame, income, debts, savings and needs for cash.
Ask how the person feels about losses and write it down in their words.
Separate must-have goals from nice-to-have goals.
Explain why a short time frame limits how much risk makes sense.
Record everything and have the client confirm it.
3.ex: A client needs a house down payment in 2 years. Because the time is short, the plan favours safer holdings and the note explains why.
3.act: Write a fact-finding form with ten questions and practise it with a partner.
3.std: Task: complete a fact-finding. Condition: a partner playing the client. Standard: goals, time frame, cash needs and risk comfort are recorded and confirmed by the partner.

4.title: Build a simple example portfolio
4.intro: Build a practice portfolio on paper to learn how parts fit. This is for study only.
pts: Explain diversification: spreading across different holdings so one problem hurts less.
Match a mix of cash, bonds and shares to a goal and time frame in a worked example.
Explain how fees reduce returns over many years.
Explain rebalancing: moving back to the planned mix when prices change it.
Write the reason for every holding in one sentence.
4.ex: Plan: 10% cash, 40% bonds, 50% shares. After a rise, shares become 58%. Rebalancing sells 8 points of shares and adds to bonds to return to the plan.
4.act: Build a practice portfolio on paper for a made-up client and write the reason for each part.
4.std: Task: build a practice portfolio. Condition: made-up client and numbers. Standard: mix fits the goal and time frame, each holding has a reason and fees are shown.

5.title: Measure results the honest way
5.intro: Results must be measured fairly and shown with the risk.
pts: Compute simple return = (end value - start value) / start value.
Explain that past results do not promise future results.
Compare a portfolio to a fair benchmark with a similar mix.
Show worst falls as well as gains.
Show results after fees.
5.ex: Start 10,000, end 10,600 after fees: return = 600 / 10,000 = 6%. In the same year the portfolio fell 9% at its worst point, and the report shows both.
5.act: Compute and report returns, fees and worst fall for a made-up portfolio over three years.
5.std: Task: write a results report. Condition: a made-up data set. Standard: numbers are correct, a benchmark is stated and risk is shown beside return.

6.title: Report, communicate and keep records
6.intro: Clients need clear reports, honest words and safe records.
pts: Write reports in plain language: what you hold, what it did, what it cost, what changes.
Never promise returns; show ranges and risks.
Keep notes of every instruction and every decision with its date.
Protect client data under privacy law; keep records for the time the regulator requires and check it.
Explain fee types and tell the client in writing.
6.ex: A client calls worried after a fall. The adviser opens the plan, shows the goal and time frame, and notes the call with date and outcome.
6.act: Write a one-page client report for the practice portfolio, with fees and risk in plain words.
6.std: Task: write a client report. Condition: one page. Standard: no promises, fees and risk shown and an eight-year-old-level summary at the top.

7.title: Manage conflicts, ethics and risk
7.intro: Trust is the product. Handle conflicts, errors and misuse of data openly.
pts: List common conflicts: commissions, own holdings, rewarding sales over fit.
Tell the client about any conflict in writing.
Have a process for errors: tell the client, fix, record the cause.
Spot fraud signs: pressure, guaranteed returns, missing documents.
Check suitability again whenever the client's life changes.
7.ex: An adviser would earn more from one fund. She tells the client and shows a comparable lower-cost option, and records the client's choice.
7.act: Write a one-page conflict and error policy and test it on two made-up cases.
7.std: Task: write a policy. Condition: one page, two cases. Standard: each case follows the policy and the record is complete.

8.title: Run a portfolio process under supervision
8.intro: Run the whole process as a learner in a safe setting: made-up or supervised cases only, under a registered professional.
pts: Work with a registered supervisor for any real client matter.
Run the cycle: fact-find, plan, build, report, review.
Review each practice portfolio every quarter on paper.
Record what went wrong and what you changed.
Write a plan for your next training step, for example the exams or registration route; check the current requirements with the regulator.
8.ex: A student runs three made-up clients for two quarters. The log shows one plan drifted from its mix. She rebalanced it and noted the reason.
8.act: Run three practice cases for two quarters and present your review to a panel.
8.std: Task: run practice cases. Condition: made-up data or a registered supervisor. Standard: the cycle is complete, records are dated and the review reasons from evidence.

quiz: What is a portfolio?
A set of investments held together for a goal.
Why check the regulator before offering a service?
Managing or advising on money for others is regulated and may need registration.
What three facts set how much risk fits?
Goals, time frame and comfort with loss.
What is diversification?
Spreading money across different holdings so one problem hurts less.
What is rebalancing?
Moving back to the planned mix after prices change it.
How do you compute simple return?
End value minus start value, divided by start value.
Why show fees and worst falls in a report?
So the client sees the true cost and risk.
What is a conflict of interest?
A situation where your gain may pull against the client's best interest.
Can you promise returns?
No; show ranges and risks.
Where should you go for your own money decisions?
A licensed professional.
